extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, poets and creative writers interested in the theory of the sublime and the beautiful
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic principles for sublime and beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies 18th‑century aesthetic principles about what produces the sublime and the beautiful (e.g., darkness, blackness, smoothness, variation, size, color, and the effects of words) for use in creative writing, criticism, or theory. Focuses on sensory/physiological causes, associative causes, and literary/poetic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkness as a source of the sublime/terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness can be a cause of the sublime because it modifies pain or terror; utter darkness makes us ignorant of our situation, exposed to unseen dangers, and thus naturally produces terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: in utter darkness we cannot know our safety, may strike obstructions, fall from precipices, or be surprised by an enemy; strength and wisdom are less protective; the bold are staggered and one prays for light. This is offered as a universal association (not merely a learned superstition) and used to rebut Locke's claim that darkness is not naturally an idea of terror. Example/allusion: invocation showing prayer for light. Anti-pattern: attributing darkness's terror solely to local storytelling (ghosts/goblins) is challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association versus intrinsic terror (ghosts/goblins objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection considered: some argue darkness becomes terrible only by association (nurse telling ghost stories). Burke argues instead that darkness is likely originally terrifying and then chosen as a fit scene for such representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: it's hard to imagine that an idea so universally terrible in all times and countries (darkness) arose only from trivial idle stories; more natural that darkness itself was an idea of terror and thus fit setting for spectral tales. Use this to distinguish learned fear from innate or widely-shared reactions when modeling emotional responses in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackness as partial darkness causing uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackness (a kind of partial darkness) can produce great uneasiness and horror independent of associative learning, illustrated by Cheselden's story of a man born blind who, on first seeing black objects and a negro woman, felt great horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anecdote is used to argue blackness has a natural, not merely associative, effect on the imagination. The example supports treating blackness in imagery as inherently capable of causing discomfort or horror. Note: blackness differs from darkness in being more confined but draws some of the same effects because of contrast with adjacent colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological eye‑strain in darkness producing pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme darkness may produce a bodily pain via mechanical strain of the iris/pupil as the eye strives for light; flashes and luminous appearances are symptoms of such spasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: as we withdraw from light the pupil enlarges; in total darkness radial fibres may contract and strain, producing a painful sensation and visual flashes. Empirical remarks: making an effort to see in darkness induces perceivable pain; working long on black ground pains eyes. Objection addressed: although the ill effects seem mental, they may originate in bodily organs whose distress transmits to the mind. Use to motivate somatic description of fear/strain in scenes of darkness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of blackness via sudden relaxation/contrast (expectation violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Black bodies are perceived as 'vacancies' among colored objects; encountering such vacuities after the eye has been kept in tension by surrounding colors causes sudden relaxation and an immediate convulsive recovery — analogous to shocks produced by unexpected physical changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: sitting on a lower chair causes violent shock; missing a stair; sudden cessation of murmuring that had induced sleep wakes the sleeper. Principle: sudden contrary change to expectation produces convulsion. Apply to visual composition: abrupt black patches among color can produce a jarring, terrifying effect; gradual presentation avoids the convulsive response. Anti-pattern: abrupt, unprepared contrast that violates sensory expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom moderates original horror of black/darkness
rubrics_metrics.description: Although black/darkness may be painful or terrible by nature, habituation softens the terror; repeated exposure makes the horror abate though a melancholy element often remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: recognition that familiarity diminishes the initial harsh effects — polished or glossy qualities of black objects can soften their sternness. Use repeated, varied exposure to a motif to temper its emotional impact in a narrative; remember the original impression persists beneath habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty produces relaxation of the system and the passion of love
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful objects cause relaxation of the solids of the system (physical signs: head reclines, eyelids half-closed, eyes roll gently, mouth slightly open, slow breath, low sigh) and this relaxation is the physical basis for the emotion of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The degree of outward physical relaxation corresponds to degree of beauty and sensibility. Reasoning is reciprocal: a beautiful object causes relaxation producing love; if love begins in the mind it will cause outward relaxation. Use for character and reader response: evoke somatic signifiers (melting, languor, softened posture) to convey beauty's effect. Note exceptions may exist, but the general rule stands as derived from repeated observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness as a principal cause of visual beauty and general relaxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness gratifies touch and tends to relax the muscular fibres; since smoothness in other senses relaxes, it is admitted as a constituent of visual beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gentle stroking with a smooth hand relieves pain, a soft well-made bed induces sleep. Visual smoothness parallels tactile smoothness: a surface that presents gentle, non-twitching impressions relaxes the sensory organs. In composition, favor surfaces and textures that imply gentle, continuous contact rather than rough or angular forms that rouse and vellicate the organs of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness (taste) as an analogue of visual beauty — smoothness of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweetness arises from smooth, fluid vehicles (water, oil) plus a 'salt' (sugar) that produces a gentle vibratory motion on the tongue; sugar particles are globular and this globularity contributes to the smooth pleasurable sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic analogy: sugar's round particles act like many small globes producing pleasant rolling sensation; water and oil are insipid but smooth and relaxing. Use cross-sensory analogies (taste↔touch↔sight) in description: sweet = smooth, and 'sweet' is metaphorically applied to visual objects. Practical implication: describe sensory experiences in ways that map smoothness across senses to enhance perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweet tastes and smells induce relaxation (sweetness relaxing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweet things, especially oily sweets and sweet smells (flowers), tend to relax and can even enfeeble the stomach or dispose one to drowsiness; languages often conflate 'soft' and 'sweet'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: milk and fruit as originally pleasant provisions for infants. Contrast: rough, pungent tastes/touches strengthen and brace the fibres. For authors: sweet imagery can be used to convey relaxation, softness, and susceptibility to love; pungent/rough imagery to convey strength, bracing, or tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation (gentle, continually varied line) as essential to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal property of beautiful objects is that the direction of their parts continually varies by very insensible deviations — never continued uniformity nor sudden sharp variation — producing a relaxing, agreeable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies and examples: gentle oscillatory motion (rocking) relaxes more than absolute rest; smoothly rising and falling surfaces produce pleasing light variations. Anti-patterns: long continued sameness tires attention; very sudden deviation (sharp angles) causes twitching or convulsion of the optic nerve and displeasure. In composition, favor gentle, flowing variation rather than rigid uniformity or abrupt angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size: smallness often compatible with beauty; greatness aligns with the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitude is relative, but generally objects greatly exceeding the ordinary size are more likely to be terrible (sublime) than beautiful; smallness per se is not hostile to beauty and can even enhance it when proportions are delicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: humming-bird's beauty enhanced by smallness; giants are naturally associated with tyranny and cruelty and are incompatible with love. Exceptions: 'fine' large objects that combine beauty qualities with large dimensions form a distinct kind. Use size intentionally: to evoke love and tenderness prefer delicate smallness; to evoke awe and terror prefer great magnitude and associated sublime qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and transparency produce pleasure via soft transmission and even reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent bodies soften transmitted light and reflect their proper color evenly; this softness of transmitted light plus even reflection produces visual pleasure analogous to tactile smoothness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: a bottle of muddy liquor whose colored rays are unevenly stopped by opaque particles produces a disagreeable effect. Composition implication: evenness of color and clarity/transparency aid beauty; the shape of the container or presentation that varies strength of color gradually can heighten the pleasure. Combine color with smooth variation to maximize visual beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words affect the passions not merely by raising precise ideas but by associative usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are divided into three sorts — aggregate (names for composed objects), simple abstract (names for single simple ideas), and compound abstract (arbitrary unions of words for complex relations). Compound abstract words (virtue, honor, persuasion) generally do not raise precise composite ideas but operate as sounds linked by habit to occasions that produced pleasure or pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for rhetoric/poetry: compound abstract words, by repeated application on occasions that affected us, come to produce similar effects without requiring the hearer to reconstruct the complex ideas they nominally denote. Use or avoid abstract terminology depending on whether you want imaginative specificity (favor concrete/aggregate words) or habitual emotive resonance (use well-conditioned abstract words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound abstract words work by association rather than imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Such words are in reality but mere sounds which, having been used on particular occasions where we received good or suffered evil, produce in the mind effects similar to those of their occasions — even after losing connection with precise ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: when striving to move passions, one can rely on the emotive power of conditioned abstract terms; but for vivid imagery and precise imagination, prefer concrete language that fosters distinct ideas. Beware that overuse of abstract words without evocative context may become empty sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: General moral words taught before particulars shape early disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Most general words, especially those denoting good and evil, are taught before the particular modes of action they refer to, and with them the love of the one and abhorrence of the other; nurses and early caretakers can imprint dispositions by seeming pleased or displeased with words or things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for character and cultural conditioning in writing: early generalized moral language can create durable affective responses in characters and readers. For persuasive writing, early framing with general moral terms can predispose audiences emotionally before particulars are supplied.
